$comment: D-MIR-DYLIB-SELF-CALL-BYPASSES-WEAK-COALESCING, the CONTROL direction. The row is about a SHARED LIBRARY whose own call to its own definition must be resolved by the LOADER rather than branched to the local body -- MEASURED 2026-09-05: a DSS-built ELF `.so` returned its OWN bodies (rc 4) where the gcc-built `.so` from identical source returned the consumer executable's (rc 6), and a DSS-built darwin dylib returned rc 1 where ld64's returned rc 2 (cycle P61, Apple Silicon). One process, two answers for one identifier, with no diagnostic anywhere. The routing that closes it is DECLARED per format (`preemptibleDefinitionBindings`), and an EXECUTABLE declares NOTHING, because the main executable is always its own winner under both loaders -- MEASURED: gcc 13.3.0 and clang 18.1.3 bind an executable's self-calls to its own weak AND strong definitions DIRECTLY, `-pie` and `-no-pie` alike, while PLT-routing the same callees in a `.so` from the same source. A corpus example cannot build a shared library and a rival consumer together, so the divergence itself is witnessed by execution outside this harness; THIS example pins the half the harness CAN carry, and it is the half that guards the cost: an executable whose self-calls were routed would pay a load through memory on every ordinary call to reach a definition nothing can replace, and on an ELF or Mach-O exec -- which cannot carry a reference resolved from the loader's global scope -- would be REFUSED outright. SHAPE: all four cells of the routing decision (weak/default, strong-global/default, `static`, hidden-visibility) are present and reached through a const function-pointer table indexed by a RUNTIME value (argc - 1), so no pass sees a constant index and no definition is dropped before the decision. What this example asserts is the exit code on both arms. The pe arm RUNS on windows, elf x86_64 on linux, elf arm64 under qemu, macho arm64 on darwin.
